books.title: Enchiridion
books.author: Epictetus
books.description: A short Stoic handbook compiled by a student of Epictetus, a former slave who became one of Rome's great teachers.
ideas: Separate what you control

Some things are up to us, our judgments, choices and efforts, and some are not, like other people's opinions or the weather. Peace comes from putting your energy into the first group and accepting the second.
dichotomy-of-control
It's our judgments that disturb us
Events themselves don't upset us; our opinions about them do. When you feel hurt, look for the judgment behind the feeling and ask whether it's true.
Want things as they are
Don't demand that events happen as you wish. Wish for them to happen as they do, and life will go smoothly. This isn't passivity; it's refusing to fight what has already happened.
Remember what things are
If you love a cup, remind yourself that it is only a cup, so you won't be crushed when it breaks. Holding things lightly lets you enjoy them without dread.
Act your part well
Life is like a play: you didn't choose your role, but you can choose to play it well. Focus on doing your part with skill rather than envying someone else's.

books.title: Meditations
books.author: Marcus Aurelius
books.description: Private notes a Roman emperor wrote to himself on how to live with virtue, calm and purpose.
ideas: Remember that you will die
The Stoics reminded themselves daily that life is short. Not to be gloomy, but to sharpen priorities: if today were among your last, would petty grudges or endless scrolling still feel worth it?
memento-mori
Prepare for difficult people
Marcus began some days by expecting to meet rude, ungrateful people. Not out of cynicism: anticipating it meant he could respond with patience instead of surprise and anger.
The obstacle becomes the way
What stands in the way of an action can itself become the material for a new action. A setback is a chance to practise patience, courage or creativity.
Retreat into yourself
People seek peace in the country or by the sea, but you can find it at any moment by turning inward. A calm mind is a retreat you carry everywhere.
Do the work of a human being
On mornings when he didn't want to get up, Marcus reminded himself that he was made to work with others, not to lie under blankets. Purpose is a better alarm than pleasure.
Everything is change
Nature loves to turn things into other things. Mountains erode, empires fall, people age. Seeing change as the normal order makes loss easier to accept.

books.title: Letters from a Stoic
books.author: Seneca
books.description: Seneca's letters to his friend Lucilius, full of practical advice on time, friendship, fear and wealth.
ideas: Life is long if you know how to use it
We don't have too little time; we waste a lot of it. Seneca urges guarding your hours as carefully as money, since time is the one thing you can't earn back.
Rehearse poverty
Set aside a few days to live on very little, eat plain food and wear rough clothes, then ask: is this what I feared? Practising hardship removes its power over you.
We suffer more in imagination
Most of what we fear never happens, and what does happen is rarely as bad as we pictured. Deal with real problems, not imagined ones.
Choose friends carefully
Spend time with people who make you better, and whom you can make better. Habits and values are contagious.
Read deeply, not widely
Skipping between many books leaves nothing behind. Stay with a few great minds, and each day take one idea to digest.

books.title: Nicomachean Ethics
books.author: Aristotle
books.description: Aristotle's foundational work on happiness, virtue and what it means to live a good life.
ideas: Happiness is an activity
For Aristotle, happiness (eudaimonia) isn't a passing mood but living well over a whole life: using your abilities fully and acting with virtue.
The golden mean
Each virtue sits between two extremes. Courage lies between cowardice and recklessness; generosity between stinginess and waste. Wisdom is finding the right amount for the situation.
We become what we repeatedly do
We become just by doing just acts and brave by doing brave acts. Character isn't something you're born with; it's built by practice until it becomes second nature.
Three kinds of friendship
Some friendships are based on usefulness, some on pleasure, and the rarest on admiring each other's character. Only the last kind survives changing circumstances.
Practical wisdom
Knowing general rules isn't enough. Practical wisdom is the skill of seeing what a particular situation calls for, and it grows with experience.

books.title: Tao Te Ching
books.author: Lao Tzu
books.description: A brief, poetic classic of Chinese philosophy about living in harmony with the natural way of things.
ideas: Be like water
Water is soft and yields to everything, yet it wears down the hardest stone. Gentleness and persistence often overcome force.
Wu wei: effortless action
Wu wei means acting without forcing, like a skilled craftsman whose work flows. Don't push against the grain of situations; find where they naturally lead.
The usefulness of emptiness
A bowl is useful because of its empty centre; a room because of its open space. What isn't there can matter as much as what is.
Knowing when enough is enough
Those who know they have enough are rich. Endless wanting is a kind of poverty no amount of wealth can cure.
The best leaders are barely noticed
When the best leader's work is done, the people say, "We did it ourselves." Great leadership empowers rather than commands.

books.title: The Republic
books.author: Plato
books.description: Plato's dialogue on justice, the ideal city and the nature of knowledge, featuring Socrates.
ideas: The allegory of the cave

Prisoners chained in a cave see only shadows and think they're reality. One escapes, sees the sun and returns, but the others mock him. Education is turning toward the light, and it can be uncomfortable.
The ring of Gyges
If you had a ring that made you invisible, would you still act justly? Plato uses this question to ask whether people are good only because they fear getting caught.
The tripartite soul
Plato saw the soul as reason, spirit and appetite, like a charioteer steering two horses. A just person lets reason guide, with spirit as its ally and appetite kept in check.
Philosopher kings
Plato argued that cities would be best ruled by those who love wisdom and don't want power. The people who seek power most eagerly are often the least fit to hold it.

books.title: Introduction to Philosophy
books.author: Nathan Smith et al. (OpenStax)
books.description: A free, peer-reviewed university textbook covering the big questions of philosophy, from logic and ethics to the mind and society.

free.note: Free from OpenStax at Rice University, online and as a PDF.

ideas: Philosophy starts with questions
Philosophy examines assumptions most people never question: what is real, what we can know, what makes an action right. Asking clearly is half the work.
Arguments have structure
An argument is a set of premises that support a conclusion. A valid argument with true premises guarantees its conclusion, which is why philosophers check both.
Three big approaches to ethics
Consequentialism judges actions by their results, deontology by duties and rules, and virtue ethics by the character they express. Each captures something the others miss.
Philosophy is global
Alongside Greek thinkers, the book covers traditions from China, India, Africa and the Americas, showing how different cultures tackled the same deep questions.
